text:
alex_m: Heads up — I'm running a Karpenter migration dry-run for GPU workloads in us-west-2. When we ramp up a few large training jobs, the cluster hits IP pressure and pods start Pending. Anyone seen this pattern with Karpenter + GPUs?

samir: Yep. ENI / IP exhaustion is the usual culprit on those instance types. GPUs + large instance families allocate fewer ENIs, so we run out of pod IPs quickly.

maya_k: Also watch AZ imbalance. If Karpenter is launching most pods into one AZ (cheapest spot), that AZ's subnets can fill even if overall vpc looks fine.

ben_p: Can you share the provisioner config? We can rate-limit or set provider.selectors to prefer instance types with higher ENI counts.

alex_m: Config excerpt I used (shortened):
```yaml
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1alpha5
kind: Provisioner
metadata:
  name: gpu-provisioner-dryrun
spec:
  requirements:
    - key: kubernetes.io/arch
      operator: In
      values: [amd64]
    - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-category
      operator: In
      values: [gpu]
  provider:
    subnetSelector: {aws_karpenter_subnet: true}
    securityGroupSelector: {karpenter_sg: true}
  consolidation:
    enabled: true
  limits:
    resources: {cpu: 2000}
```

samir: consolidation.enabled helps long-term costs but can trigger pod churn. For noisy GPU queues I usually set consolidation: enabled=false during migration canaries.

maya_k: Another lever — set provisioner.spec.ttlSecondsUntilExpired lower so Karpenter removes empty ephemeral nodes faster, but be careful: that can interact with eviction thresholds and training checkpoints.

ben_p: We saw better results when we:
- pre-warmed a small pool of dedicated GPU nodegroups for burst fallback
- limited Karpenter to one AZ to control IP distribution during tests
- used instance types with 8+ ENIs for pod density (traded some cost for IPs)

alex_m: Devops-bot just pushed an alert during the run: 
devops-bot: ALERT: subnet-usw2a-ml (10.0.32.0/27) IP utilization 88% — new pod provisioning failing, retrying fallback.

sre-oncall: Logs show CNI error: "failed to assign IP: no free addresses". Karpenter attempted to create 6 nodes quickly; each node only allowed 4 pods due to ENI limits.

samir: Quick checks: run `kubectl get nodes -o wide` and `kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending` to see which nodes are blocking. For AWS details: `aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters Name=subnet-id,Values=<id>`

maya_k: Mitigation ideas we discussed:
- increase subnet size or add secondary subnets (fast but requires infra change)
- enable prefix delegation / prefix allocation for VPC CNI (if not already)
- use smaller instance types with more ENIs per vCPU ratio
- pre-create a managed nodegroup as a fallback (spot/interruption-friendly)

ben_p: For cost: pre-warming a tiny dedicated pool adds a predictable baseline cost but avoids expensive retries and fallbacks. Karpenter can then be allowed to scale over that baseline.

alex_m: Is there a recommended Karpenter setting to throttle node creation speed? I couldn't find a global rate limiter.

samir: No single knob currently. We combine: `limits.resources` on the provisioner, adjust `consolidation` and `ttlSecondsUntilExpired`, and use admission/queue shaping on our scheduler side. Also use `ttlSecondsAfterEmpty` to avoid too many spin-ups.

maya_k: Example: set limits.resources.cpu smaller during canary so Karpenter won't create 20 nodes at once. Also set `provider.capacityType` to prefer on-demand for a small baseline pool.

alex_m: Good action items: 1) add a tiny pre-warm managed nodegroup in each AZ for GPUs, 2) adjust provisioner limits for canary, 3) coordinate subnet sizing with infra (or enable prefix assignment). I'll open a runbook PR.

ben_p: +1. Also add a test that simulates IP pressure so future migrations don't surprise infra.

sre-oncall: I'll create a short incident playbook entry: how to detect IP exhaustion vs real scheduling failures and quick mitigation commands.

alex_m: Thanks — I'll post the PR link when ready. :thumbsup:
